The Models

Considerations

The main tricky obstacle to modelling total-points-scored is the possibility of overtime; even though there are normally 48 minutes in an NBA game (“regulation” time) and this occurs about 94% of the time, if the score is tied at the end of the 48 minutes, another 5 minutes is added on the clock. If the score is tied at the end of the extra 5 minutes, another 5 minutes is added and so on. Thus, if you fit a naive regression model modelling total-points-scored, you’ll see some deviations in your residuals which will clearly violate normality.

Two competing strategies were used to get around this; the first, was to model points-per-48 minutes and probability of overtime separately, and once posterior-draws for both were obtained, to recombine for a joint-posterior of raw total points (basically a normal-mixture). As well, since total points scored can only take on positive integer values and since the over-dispersed Poisson model tends to handle skewed-distributions quite effectively, an over-dispersed Poisson (i.e. the ‘qausi’-Poisson) model was fit for comparison. Bets are only placed when the two models both agree a bet is worth it.

A secondary obstacle is that there are hundreds of games being played for any given season, but only 30 teams; the total-points-scored in one game by a team is NOT independent of the total-points-scored in another game by the same team. The strategy to address this was to include random intercepts (one per each team-within-season) in the stacked model in addition to the weights.

Notation

\[ Y: \text{total points scored by home and away team combined in a single NBA game} \\ Y_{per48}: \text{total points scored by home and away team combined in a single NBA game, per 48 minutes} \\ \hat{Y}_{Vegas}: \text{Vegas's over-under} \\ Home: \text{Home team} \\ Away: \text{Away team} \\ f(X,\beta): \text{Unknown-but-true data-generating function for unobserved parameters of interest } \\ \gamma: \text{Random intercepts for points-per-48 minutes by team, with a unique variance component per season} \\ v: \text{Random intercepts for log-odds of overtime/double-overtime by team, with variance component shared across all seasons} \\ u: \text{Random intercepts for log-points scored by team, with a unique variance component per season} \\ \sigma^2_{\{ \cdot \}}: \text{Variance component indexed by } \{ \cdot \} \text{ depending on model} \]

Note, the same random effects for a team are preserved over the season such that for home games, its random intercept is the “home” random intercept, and for away games, it’s random intercept is the “away” intercept.

Model 1

The first model being considered is essentially a normal-mixture; points-per-48 minutes was modeled via a normal distribution, and overtime modeled as a categorical distribution with outcomes regulation (no overtime), single overtime, and double overtime (higher overtimes are very very rare).

Random intercepts are included for both the home team and away team in each model; random intercepts are nested by season for pts-per-48 minutes, such that each season is assigned its own unique random-effect variance component; this is because each year since 2010, both variability and total-points scored has increased. There are 390 unique team-year random intercepts being “predicted” for points-per-48 and total-points outcomes, implying that 780 are required for modelling overtime.

For modelling overtime, a single random-effect variance component was shared across all seasons; the variability in overtime does not change much year-to-year, although it is true some teams seem more prone to overtime than others.

\[ Y = Y_{per48}(1_{regulation} + (1+\frac{5}{48})1_{overtime} + (1+\frac{10}{48})1_{double-overtime}) \\ E[Y] = E[Y_{per48}](1 + \frac{5}{48}\hat{p}_{overtime} + \frac{10}{48}\hat{p}_{double-overtime}) \]

Breaking this down into its first part, modeling points scored per-48 minutes with Gaussian-distributed error terms,

\[ Y_{per48} = f(X,\beta) + \gamma_{Home} + \gamma_{Away} + \epsilon_{per48} \\ \epsilon_{per48} \sim N(0,\sigma^2_{per48}) \\ \gamma \sim N(0,\sigma^2_{\gamma_{season}}) \]

For the second part, recall from the simulations that for categorical outcomes (with \(K=3\) in this case) the random effect coefficients take on the form of diagonal 2x2 matrices, which for convenience, are assumed to be independent. Essentially, the number of random effects for \(K=3\) outcomes is double that of regular binary outcomes with \(K=2\).

\[ (1_{regulation},1_{overtime},1_{double-overtime}) \sim Cat(p_{regulation},p_{overtime},p_{double-overtime}) \\ (p_{regulation},p_{overtime},p_{double-overtime}) \sim Dir(1-\frac{e^{\eta_{overtime}} +e^{\eta_{double-overtime}}}{1+e^{\eta_{overtime}}+e^{\eta_{double-overtime}}},\frac{e^{\eta_{overtime}}}{1+e^{\eta_{overtime}}+e^{\eta_{double-overtime}}}, \frac{e^{\eta_{double-overtime}}}{1+e^{\eta_{overtime}}+e^{\eta_{double-overtime}}}) \\ (\eta_{overtime},\eta_{double-overtime}) = f(X,\beta) + v_{Home} + v_{Away} \\ v_{j=1...M} = (v_{j_{overtime}},v_{j_{double-overtime}})_{j=1...M} \sim N_2(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix} \sigma^2_{v} & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma^2_{v} \end{pmatrix}) \]

Model 2

The second model is much simpler; irrelevant of overtime, the points scored in the NBA game is modeled with a quasi-poisson “distribution”, i.e., we assume \(Y \sim Pois(\phi\lambda)\).

I fix \(\phi\) to be degenerate at its MLE value (i.e. the value obtained from the Newton-Raphson procedure, MLE is a misnomer) for purposes of deriving both a posterior distribution for \(\sigma^2_{\hat{\eta}}\) and a posterior-predictive distribution, which works well, but theoretically speaking I should probably assign a prior on it and integrate it out. But I feel like that kind of ruins the whole “quasi”-spirit, as you just end up with a negative-binomial distribution setting a gamma prior on the dispersion parameter anyways.

While normally the quasi-likelihood doesn’t require so many steps, we need to be able to connect it back to a real likelihood for purposes of generating posterior-predictive draws and evaluating damp-step improvement; hence, the distribution of \(\frac{Y}{\phi}\) is derived explicitly below, rather than just conveniently requiring it’s expectation and variance as per-usual with quasi-likeilhood.

\[ If \ Y \sim Pois(\phi \lambda = e^{\eta + \log \phi}) \\ Then \ \Rightarrow E[\frac{Y}{\phi}] = \lambda = e^{\eta} \\ And \ \Rightarrow V[\frac{Y}{\phi}] = \frac{\phi \lambda}{\phi^2} = \frac{e^{\eta}}{\phi} \\ The \ Canonical-REF \ model \ that \ satisfies \ this \ is, \\ P(\frac{Y}{\phi}) = exp(\frac{\frac{Y}{\phi}\eta -e^{\eta}}{\phi})c(Y,\phi) \\ = exp(\frac{Y(\eta + \log(\phi))-e^{\eta + log(\phi)}}{\phi^2})e^{-\frac{Ylog(\phi)}{\phi^2}}c(Y,\phi) \\ = exp(\frac{Y(\eta + \log(\phi))-e^{\eta + log(\phi)}}{\phi^2})c^*(Y,\phi) \\ \propto exp(\frac{Y\eta^*-e^{\eta^*}}{\phi^2}) \\ \eta^* = f(X,\beta) + u_{Home} + u_{Away} \\ u_{j=1...M} \sim N(0,\sigma^2_{u_{season}}) \\ \phi \sim degenerate \ where \ \phi = \hat{\phi}_{MLE} \]

With the above formulation, we can still make draws from an explicit parametric distribution for purposes of deriving a posterior predictive distribution (by back transforming draws from the quasi-poisson outcome \(\frac{Y}{\phi}\) to \(Y\)), but we only need to specify the first two moments of the log-likelihood (the score and the information) as well as a function proportional to the likelihood (for purposes of evaluating newton-raphson damp-step improvement) when finding weights for the stacked model.

Priors

All prior beliefs for predicting future observations are expressed as normal distributions on the link-function scale (i.e. log-odds of overtime for categorical regression, log points-per-game for Poisson regression, raw points-per-48-minutes for linear regression). This is because the parameter \(\sigma^2_{\hat{\eta}}\) is quantified based on the discrepancy between the stacked model’s linear-predictor and the true function of unknown parameters \(\textit{on the link function scale}\). It also allows one to take advantage of the closed-form posterior distributions provided by normal-normal conjugacy.

For setting a prior the expected points-per-48 min, we use the reported over/under of Vegas (\(\hat{Y}_{Vegas}\)) multiplied by (48/48.34) as the mean, and the variability in the observed Vegas-residuals over past years on the absolute scale, multiplied by (48/48.34)^2, as the average amount of minutes per NBA game is 48.34 minutes. This yielded a variance of about 350.715.

\[ \eta_{per48} \sim N(\hat{Y}_{Vegas}(\frac{48}{48.34}),\sigma^2_{\hat{Y}_{Vegas}}(\frac{48}{48.34})^2) \]

For setting a prior on overtime, it’s a little trickier because we can’t leverage the information that Vegas presents as straightforwardly as their over/under (actually, you can based on the Skellam distribution and looking at the spread, but that’s for another time). My approach, was to set a normal prior distribution for the log-odds of overtime and double-overtime on the link-function scale centered around the logit-transformed overall, \(\textit{marginal}\) probabilities of overtime and double-overtime in the NBA (approximately 0.0520 and 0.0082) respectively. The variability of this normal distribution is the same as my model’s posterior \(\sigma^2_{\hat{\eta}}\); I consider the overall probability of overtime(s), and my model’s predicted probability of overtimes(s), as equally informative.

\[ (\eta_{overtime},\eta_{double-overtime}) \sim N_2( \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\log[0.0518]}{1-\log[0.0518] -\log[0.0082]} &\frac{\log[0.0082]}{1-\log[0.0518] - \log [.0082]} \end{pmatrix} ,\begin{pmatrix} \sigma^2_{\hat{\eta}_{v}} & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma^2_{\hat{\eta}_{v}}\end{pmatrix}) \]

Finally, for the quasi-poisson model, we use the prior based on the figure presented in the introduction.

\[ \eta_{logPts} \sim N(\log\hat{Y}_{Vegas},\sigma^2_{\log\hat{Y}_{Vegas}}) \]

At this point, enough information is provided such that all the of steps needed to derive the posterior-predictive distributions I laid out earlier can be implemented, the code for which I have online for reference.

    glm_pca_logPtsGame,
    glm_pca_ptsGame,
    earth_2degree, 
file = 'candidate_models.RData')

Running these models and generating posterior distributions all at once usually takes between 12-24 hours, depending on how many posterior draws I want. Modeling overtime as a 3-category outcome usually takes up over 2/3rds of this computational time. This of course, all depends on how many models are being stacked and how many are ultimately selected by the backwards base-learner selection procedure, but the wrapper for rstan quantify_stacked_uncertainty is by far the most time-intensive part.

The following code is what I usually run overnight, although admittedly because it’s so intensive, I just run the categorical model on my school computer instead (strictly for academic reasons of course).

Placing Bets

Inputting Priors

The only actual daily physical task I need to do to place bets is to type in the over under set by Vegas and hit ctrl+enter. My R script will automatically webscrape NBA data from last-night’s games (or any previous games I missed), clean and process it, load my pre-trained models, make predictions on the new data, generate Metropolis-Hastings MCMC draws based on those predictions, and print out results telling me to whether to bet or not.

Checking Posterior-Predictives

For generating posterior draws, I use little more than the MH function we turned in for homework recently. Obviously there are a lot of moving parts, but I think showing this snippet might convince you that the burdensome notation betrays the simplicity of what’s actually happening.

This is for the points-per-48 minutes outcome.

if(F){
######### Empirical smoothed-densities of posterior draws ##
  ## posterior draws of variance parameters
posterior_draws <- cbind(c(stan.result@sim$samples[[1]]$dispersion[-c(1:10000)],
                           stan.result@sim$samples[[2]]$dispersion[-c(1:10000)]),
                         c(stan.result@sim$samples[[1]]$sigmaSq_etahat[-c(1:10000)],
                           stan.result@sim$samples[[2]]$sigmaSq_etahat[-c(1:10000)]))

######### Distributions for new data #######################
  ## formulas for computing the joint posterior 
closest_density <- function(v,dens){
  diff <- abs(dens[,1]-v)
  dens[,2][which(diff == min(diff))]/sum(dens[,2])
}
f_y_given_eta <- function(Y,eta,dispersion){
  sum((dnorm(Y,mean = eta, sd = sqrt(dispersion),log = T)))
}
f_etahat_given_y_eta_sigmaSqhateta <- f_y_given_eta
prior_eta <- function(eta,mu0,sigmaSq0){
  sum((dnorm(eta,mean = mu0*(48/48.324), sd = sqrt(sigmaSq0)*48/48.324,log = T)))
}
sigmaSq0 <- var(vegas_resid)*(48/avg_time)^2
density_sigmaSqetahat <- cbind(density(posterior_draws[,2])$x,
                               density(posterior_draws[,2])$y)
density_dispersion <- cbind(density(posterior_draws[,1])$x,
                            density(posterior_draws[,1])$y)
post_eta <- function(sigmaSq_0,
                     sigmaSq,
                     mu_0,
                     x_i,
                     eta){
  new_mu <- 1/(1/sigmaSq_0 + 1/sigmaSq) * 
    (mu_0/sigmaSq_0 + x_i/sigmaSq)
  
  new_sig <- sqrt(
    1/(1/sigmaSq_0+ 1/sigmaSq)
  )
  
  dnorm(eta,mean = new_mu, sd = new_sig,log = T)
}
######### START MH for new data #############################
post_predictive_draws <- list()
for(k in 1:length(vegas_preds)){
  print(k)
  initial_values <- c("eta" = vegas_preds[k]*(48/avg_time),
                      "Ynew" = as.numeric((my_preds_per48[k])),
                      
                      "dispersion" = sum(density_dispersion[,1]*density_dispersion[,2])/sum(density_dispersion[,2]),
                      "sigmaSq_etahat" = sum(density_sigmaSqetahat[,1]*density_sigmaSqetahat[,2])/sum(density_sigmaSqetahat[,2]))
  M <- initial_values
  result <- foreach(chain = 1:5,.combine = 'rbind') %do% {
    print("")
    res_temp <- try({(foreach(i = 1:48000,
             .combine = 'rbind') %dopar% {
               MM <- try({MH_update(
                 M,
                 f = function(x) {
                     log(closest_density(x['dispersion'],density_dispersion)) +
                     log(closest_density(x['sigmaSq_etahat'],density_sigmaSqetahat)) +
                     f_y_given_eta(x['Ynew'], x['eta'],x['dispersion']) + 
                     post_eta(sigmaSq0,
                              x['sigmaSq_etahat']+x['dispersion'], ## we add dispersion when marginalizing over Y
                              vegas_preds[k],
                              my_preds_per48[k],
                              x['eta'])
                 },
                 g = function(from,to,sd_prop = c(4,10,2,1,1)){
                   sum(log(dnorm(to,from,sd_prop)))
                 },
                 g.s = function(from,sd_prop = c(4,10,2,1,1)){
                   from + rnorm(length(from),
                                0,
                                sd_prop)
                 },
                 log = T)},silent = T)
               if(class(MM) != 'try-error'){
                 Mprev <- M
                 M <- MM
                 if(any(M != Mprev)){
                   M
                 } else{
                   invisible()
                 }
               } else {
                 M <- M + rnorm(length(M),
                                0,
                                0.01)
               }
             })},silent = T)
    if(class(res_temp) != 'try-error'){
      ## burn-in the first 4th
      res_temp <- res_temp[-c(1:(nrow(res_temp)/4)),]
      ## only select every 2nd (thinning)
      res_temp[seq(1,nrow(res_temp),by = 2),]
    }
  }
  post_predictive_draws[[k]] <- result[,2]
  plot(post_predictive_draws[[k]],
       main = paste0("M.H. Draws for Total Points Scored per 48 Min: ",
                     paste(matchups_enter[k,1:2],collapse = " vs. "),
                                     collapse = ""))
}
stopCluster(cl)
######### END MH #############
}

Modeling Spread and Moneyline

Briefly, the spread is the difference in points between the home team and away team at the end of the game, and you can bet whether you think a team will win by more or less points than another team. The moneyline is just betting on who will win or lose. These are fun outcomes to model by themselves, but frankly I’m done modeling because spending time with my family and friends is more important. It also involves modeling a Skellam distribution https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skellam_distribution, which isn’t easily incorporated into the AbsolutelyStacked pipeline. Fortunately, there is a shortcut.

I argue, once we have posterior draws for total points scored, we have everything we need to derive posterior-predictive distributions for spread and moneyline too.

Knowing the over/under and spread, we can easily reconstruct the total points that Vegas predicted the home team to score \((Y_{Home})\)

\[ Y_{Home} = \frac{(Y_{Home} - Y_{Away}) +(Y_{Home} + Y_{Away})}{2} \\ \hat{Y}_{Home}= \frac{(Spread) +(Over/Under)}{2} \\ \hat{\theta}_{Vegas} = \log(\frac{\frac{\hat{Y}_{Home}}{(\hat{Y}_{Home} + \hat{Y}_{Away})}}{1-\frac{\hat{Y}_{Home}}{(\hat{Y}_{Home} + \hat{Y}_{Away})}}) = \log(\hat{{Y}}_{Home})-\log(\hat{{Y}}_{Away}) \]

Conveniently, Vegas’s residuals of the logit-proportion of home team points scored is again, well-approximated by normality.

The posterior-predictive distribution for the spread is then straightforward to derive. We already have the marginal, posterior-predictive distribution for total points scored; and now we have a direct prior on the logit-proportion of points scored by the home team, conditional upon total points scored. Finally, we know that these are \(\textit{orthogonal}\) outcomes (the sample size tells us nothing about the proportion, the proportion tells us nothing about the sample size), so they are independent. A simple 4-step algorithm provides us with posterior draws of the spread.

\[ 1) \text{ Sample } Y^{New} \text{ from } P(Y^{New}|\cdot) \text{ the posterior-predictive distribution of total points} \\ 2) \text{ Sample } \theta^{New} \text{ from } P(\theta^{New}) \sim N(\hat{\theta}^{New}_{Vegas},\sigma_{\hat{\theta}_{Vegas}}) \\ 3) \text{ Compute } Y^{New}_{Home} = (\frac{e^{\theta^{New}}}{1+e^{\theta^{New}}})*Y^{New} \\ 4) \text{ Compute } Y^{New}_{Home}-Y^{New}_{Away} = 2Y^{New}_{Home}-Y^{New} \]

Obviously, if we have a posterior-predictive distribution for the difference in points between the home team and away team, we immediately have a posterior-predictive distribution for the probability of the home team winning or losing, and so we can place informed moneyline bets as well. The point is, once we have total points modeled, we can make all 3 types of the most popular bets rather than having to re-model everything from scratch.

Conclusion

Interpretation

A key philosophy that makes this all possible (or not possible, if you disagree) is the strong likelihood principle; the belief that all of the information in a sample is communicated by its likelihood.

A proof presented by Dr. Breheny on the first day of Likelihood Theory gives some mathematical insight into why people might think this; https://myweb.uiowa.edu/pbreheny/7110/wiki/likelihood-is-minimal-sufficient.html.

If you subscribe to the strong likelihood principle, then you don’t need to know anything about the training data other than it’s likelihood, as this contains “all” of the information in the sample. Whether or not the model is tractable (a stacked model certainly isn’t), the likelihood doesn’t care; all that is needed to compute the likelihood are the observed values, the fitted values, and if relevant, the exponential dispersion parameter. Maybe it isn’t easily interpretable or tractable, but depending on your task, that might not matter. Once we have the likelihood, we can use information-theoretic AIC backwards selection to choose the best combination of base learners, a permuted likelihood-ratio statistic for evaluating variable importance, and Bayesian posterior-predictive distributions for making decisions. As long as we can partition really complicated or difficult-to-model outcomes into its orthogonal sub-components (for example, a Skellam distribution with correlated outcomes into a normal GLM for total-points-per-48 minutes, a categorical GLM for number of minutes, and a binomial GLM for proportion-of-points-scored by home team), we can use the stacked likelihood to glue it all back together with \(\textit{no loss of information}\), using whatever big-black-box models and fancy normalization schemes we desire.

One way stacking can then be interpreted is from the perspective of feature reduction; once trained, out-of-fold predictions of base learners are deterministic functions that map from higher-dimensions into single vectors of predictions (matrices for categorical outcomes), predictions that when link-function transformed, are well approximated by a linear-relationship with the outcome of interest, making it easy for a GLM to model (and easy for us to compute the likelihood). Since all of the information in the sample is communicated through the likelihood, \(\textit{philosphically}\) speaking, there’s no actual loss-of-information happening when we stack, and so all of that complicated nasty non-linear happenings in the data can still be explained with the same GLM models we statisticians prefer, all captured by just a \(\textit{few parsimonious covariates}\), i.e., the base-learner predictions.

Another way stacking can be interpreted is from a Bayesian perspective; note that on the simulations, we sometimes achieved marginally better performance with the constrained coefficients than the unconstrained….. not that the unconstrained MLEs didn’t perform well, just that \(\textit{knowing ahead of time}\) the lower bounds and sum of the coefficients obviously helped the constrained MLEs achieve better estimates.

Hence, the sum-to-one and non-negativity constraint is simply an improper prior; and that’s why we find the unconstrained MLEs first, and why finding the constrained weights is referred to as \(\textit{updating}\). The MLE weights are sufficient for capturing the out-of-fold likelihood, the prior distribution is the constraint, so the constrained weights are actually MAP estimates.

\[ P(\beta|\hat{\beta}_{MLE}) \propto P(\hat{\beta}_{MLE}|\beta)P(\beta) \\ P(\beta) \sim 1_{\sum^p_j {\beta_j} = 1, \beta_j \geq 0 \forall j} \]

This helps illustrate the connection to penalized regression as well; consider, as we saw, the weights tend to be non-negative anyways when we have a parsimonious set of base-learners, so this constraint is easily satisfied. The only constraint left is the sum-to-one, which is equivalently formulated as follows.

\[ P(\beta) \sim 1_{\sum^p_j {\beta_j} = 1} \equiv P(\beta) \sim 1_{\sum^p_j { |\beta_j |} = 1} \]

This accomplishes the same task as LASSO; except instead of using cross-validation to find the penalty term or a more direct approach, we are simply defining it explicitly to be whatever happens to satisfy the sum-to-one constraint (you can confirm this by looking at the Lagrangian terms returned by quadprog and Rsolnp as well).

As was shown theoretically and empirically, we have a lot of good reasons to think that this prior distribution (the sum-to-one and non-negativity constraint) holds true. By far the most common procedure on Kaggle and the literature for selecting weights is using LASSO as the meta-learner, tuned with cross-validation (which requires nested cross-validation). At the very least, the approach presented here suggests this is unnecessary; we already have a pretty good idea of what the penalty should be, and it’s whatever happens to satisfy the sum-to-one constraint.

Because I’ve included an l2-norm penalty term as well, you can technically use AbsolutelyStacked to fit the equivalent-of elastic-net models (under the very special circumstance that the coefficients are all of the same sign) although I wouldn’t particularly recommend it as the easiest option for doing so; tuning would be performed for the l2-norm penalty and the sum constraint (which implies a certain l1-penalty).

Apparently, you can use quadratic programming to fit proper l1-norm regularized models as well https://www.erikdrysdale.com/l1_solution/.

Final Thoughts

It may seem like a lot, but I sincerely believe I did about the bare minimum of what I needed to do in order to obtain a valid method of betting on NBA games that was actually powerful enough to \(\textit{sometimes}\) allow me to make bets.

If I have learned anything from this project, it is that being a good subjective Bayesian is like being a good partner in a relationship; it requires honesty, trust, being sensitive to different viewpoints, and paying attention to the little things, even when it gets complicated. As well, model-averaging is mathematical proof that bringing together a diversity of different ideas will improve predictive performance while echo chambers, with high-covariance between base learners, will prove otherwise.

Thank you so much for reading, it honestly means the world to me if (somehow) you got this far

Matt
